title: Jump Game II
interviewTips: Clarify guarantee: can you assume last index is always reachable? Yes per statement, so no -1 case.
Trade-off: O(n^2) DP is easy to derive but TLE for n=10^4; O(n) greedy with farthest and currentEnd is expected.
Edge-case tip: n==1 needs 0 jumps; do not count an extra jump when you start at target, and loop only to n-2 in greedy.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Brute Force DP
approaches.intuition: If we know minimum jumps to reach every earlier index j, then minimum jumps to reach i is 1 plus the best j that can jump directly to i. Compute left to right.
approaches.theory: Define dp[i] as min jumps to reach i. dp[0]=0, dp[i]=INF initially. For i from 1 to n-1, for j < i, if j+nums[j] >= i then dp[i]=min(dp[i], dp[j]+1). This is DAG shortest path where edge j->k exists if k <= j+nums[j]. Correct by optimal substructure: any optimal path to i comes via some predecessor j, so taking min over all feasible j is optimal.

timeComplexity.explanation: For each i we scan all j < i, total n*(n-1)/2 checks.

edgeCases: nums=[5,0,0,0,0,1] tests long jump from start

approaches.name: Approach 2: BFS Level Order
approaches.intuition: Each jump is an edge from i to (i+1 .. i+nums[i]). Minimum jumps equals shortest path in unweighted graph, which BFS finds level by level.
approaches.theory: Start BFS queue with 0. Each BFS level corresponds to one more jump. Expand node cur to all unvisited nxt in (cur+1 .. cur+nums[cur]). First time we reach n-1 we used minimal jumps by BFS property. Visited prevents reprocessing. Correct but naive expansion can be O(n^2) in worst case like all 1s with large n, though each node enqueued once.

timeComplexity.complexity: O(n^2) worst-case, O(n) with range optimization
timeComplexity.explanation: Each node dequeued once but naive inner loop scans all neighbors; sum of out-degrees can be O(n^2). Can be optimized to O(n) by tracking max visited.

steps: expand 1 -> reach 4 includes target, return jumps=2

approaches.name: Approach 3: Optimal Greedy Range Expansion
approaches.intuition: We do not need to know exact landing spot, only how far the current number of jumps can reach. Extend the frontier as far as possible, then take one more jump.
approaches.theory: Maintain farthest reachable with jumps+1 jumps and currentEnd = farthest reachable with jumps jumps. Iterate i in [0, n-2]: farthest=max(farthest, i+nums[i]). When i==currentEnd, we must use another jump to progress, so jumps++, currentEnd=farthest. This is implicit BFS: all indices in (prevEnd, currentEnd] are one jump away. Greedy is optimal because farthest is the maximum over all i in current window, so no choice with same jumps can go further.

timeComplexity.explanation: Single pass to n-1, O(1) work per index.

steps: i=2: farthest=4, i==curEnd -> jumps=2 curEnd=4 break

edgeCases: nums=[1,2,3] -> jumps=2, tests loop bound n-1 to avoid extra count
